front_blocks.md: Define the **septum**.

back_blocks.md: The **septum** is the muscular wall separating the left and right sides of the heart, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.

front_blocks.md: What is the function of the **coronary arteries**?

back_blocks.md: They lie on the surface of the heart and supply the **heart muscle** itself with **oxygenated blood**.

front_blocks.md: Why are the **ventricle** walls thicker than the **atrial** walls?

back_blocks.md: The **ventricles** pump blood much further, so they need more **muscle** to generate a higher **pressure**.
The **atria** only pump blood into the ventricles just below them.

cards.front_md: Why are the **ventricle** walls thicker than the **atrial** walls?
cards.back_md:
The **ventricles** pump blood much further, so they need more **muscle** to generate a higher **pressure**.

The **atria** only pump blood into the ventricles just below them.

front_blocks.md: Why is the **left ventricle** wall thicker than the **right**?

back_blocks.md: The **left ventricle** pumps blood around the **whole body**, so it must generate a much higher **pressure**.
The **right ventricle** only pumps to the **lungs**, which are close by and would be damaged by high pressure.

The pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood away from the heart.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The **pulmonary artery** carries **deoxygenated** blood from the **right ventricle** to the lungs.

front_blocks.md: Why do the **ventricles** have thicker walls than the **atria**?

back_blocks.md: The ventricles must generate a **higher pressure** to pump blood out of the heart.
The atria only pump blood a **short distance** into the ventricles.

cards.front_md: Why do the **ventricles** have thicker walls than the **atria**?
cards.back_md:
The ventricles must generate a **higher pressure** to pump blood out of the heart.

The atria only pump blood a **short distance** into the ventricles.

front_blocks.md: Why is the wall of the **left ventricle** thicker than that of the **right ventricle**?

back_blocks.md: The left ventricle pumps blood at **high pressure** all around the body (systemic circulation).
The right ventricle only pumps blood a short distance to the **lungs**, at lower pressure.

cards.front_md: Why is the wall of the **left ventricle** thicker than that of the **right ventricle**?
cards.back_md:
The left ventricle pumps blood at **high pressure** all around the body (systemic circulation).

The right ventricle only pumps blood a short distance to the **lungs**, at lower pressure.

front_blocks.md: Why must the **right ventricle** pump blood at a **lower pressure**?

back_blocks.md: High pressure would **damage the delicate lung capillaries** and force out too much tissue fluid.

cards.front_md: Why must the **right ventricle** pump blood at a **lower pressure**?

front_blocks.md: What happens during **atrial systole**?

back_blocks.md: The **atria contract**, pushing the remaining blood into the ventricles.
The **atrioventricular valves are open**.

cards.front_md: What happens during **atrial systole**?
cards.back_md:
The **atria contract**, pushing the remaining blood into the ventricles.

The **atrioventricular valves are open**.

front_blocks.md: What happens to the valves during **ventricular systole**?

back_blocks.md: Rising ventricular pressure closes the **atrioventricular valves**.
When ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, the **semilunar valves open** and blood is forced out.

cards.front_md: What happens to the valves during **ventricular systole**?
cards.back_md:
Rising ventricular pressure closes the **atrioventricular valves**.

When ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, the **semilunar valves open** and blood is forced out.

front_blocks.md: What causes the **semilunar valves to close**?

back_blocks.md: During **diastole**, ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure.
The higher arterial pressure pushes the semilunar valves shut, preventing backflow.

front_blocks.md: Define the **sinoatrial node (SAN)**.

back_blocks.md: The **sinoatrial node** is the heart's **pacemaker**, in the wall of the right atrium, which sets the heart rate.

front_blocks.md: What is the role of the **sinoatrial node (SAN)**?

back_blocks.md: It generates a **wave of electrical excitation** that spreads across both **atria**, causing them to contract.

cards.front_md: What is the role of the **sinoatrial node (SAN)**?

front_blocks.md: Define the **atrioventricular node (AVN)**.

back_blocks.md: The **atrioventricular node** lies between the atria and ventricles; it **delays** the impulse before passing it to the ventricles.

cards.front_md: Define the **atrioventricular node (AVN)**.
cards.back_md: The **atrioventricular node** lies between the atria and ventricles; it **delays** the impulse before passing it to the ventricles.

front_blocks.md: Why is there a **delay** at the atrioventricular node?

back_blocks.md: The delay ensures the **atria finish contracting** and empty completely **before** the ventricles contract.

cards.front_md: Why is there a **delay** at the atrioventricular node?
cards.back_md: The delay ensures the **atria finish contracting** and empty completely **before** the ventricles contract.

front_blocks.md: What is the role of the **Purkyne tissue**?

back_blocks.md: It conducts the wave of excitation down the **septum** to the **apex** of the heart.
This makes the ventricles contract from the **apex upwards**, pushing blood up towards the arteries.
